description: Команда True Aura Farmers - хочемо створити інтерактивну карту, яка допоможе побачити й зрозуміти зміни поверхні Землі за радарними даними NASA NISAR. Один із можливих сценаріїв — порівняти територію до та після повені, визначити ймовірно затоплені ділянки й показати масштаб змін.
summary:
SilvaSAR is an interactive, open-source application with web visualization that uses radar data from the NISAR satellite and the Earthdata world map. It automatically processes downloaded data according to the selected filters and delivers an analysis of landscape changes: HV backscatter changes, forest growth and clearing, biomass growth, and more.

SilvaSAR has a user-friendly interface with clear functions. Using it is very simple: select the parameters you need in the toolbar on the left, click “Download and process,” and get the result. Different views of the result can be switched at the top center of the map.

Checking changes in specific areas requires NISAR data and processing it yourself. Without the necessary experience, this is difficult and takes a lot of time, which is often in short supply. Our application takes this work on, leaving more time for analysis and decision-making for educators, scientists, and people of various professions.
details:
What SilvaSAR Does

SilvaSAR (from the Latin silva, “forest”, and SAR, Synthetic Aperture Radar) is an open-source radar forest guard. It finds forest loss, and other surface changes such as water-related ones, from NISAR (the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar mission, a joint project of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration of the USA and the Indian Space Research Organisation) data in the L-band, and shows the result on an interactive map. The typical test area is in the Carpathians near Chernivtsi, Ukraine.

The L-band wavelength is 24 cm, so the signal passes through cloud and the upper canopy and responds to trunks, branches and the ground. When trees are cut, volume scattering in the cross-polarized HV channel (horizontal transmit, vertical receive) usually drops by several decibels. Optical satellites cannot see this through cloud or in darkness.

How It Works, Step by Step

  1. Pick your territory. Enter coordinates (West, South, East, North, in degrees) or right-click the map and choose “Set area centre here”, then set the half-size in kilometres.
  2. Find the scenes. The app searches the NASA ASF (Alaska Satellite Facility) archive for NISAR scenes over the area. It lists the available radars and orbit tracks (ascending, when the satellite moves south to north, and descending, when it moves north to south) with the number of scenes and dates. A free NASA Earthdata login is needed only for downloading, and the password is not stored.
  3. Choose the mode.
    • Pair of dates: one “before” and one “after” image are downloaded and compared.
    • Time series: all dates between “before” and “after” are processed, and each date is compared with the previous one. Dynamics become visible, and one-off disturbances (rain, wet snow) are flagged.
  4. Decide what to look for. Select the polarization (HV, HH or the HV/HH ratio), the smoothing filter and the analysis mode (for example, clearing and gain). Thresholds, minimum patch size and the forest threshold are adjustable.
  5. Process the data. The app downloads scenes with resume support and processes only the area of interest. It removes the whole-scene shift (for example, caused by wet soil) and counts loss only inside forest, using a forest mask based on the “before” image.
  6. Read the results. Changes are grouped into patches. Loss is shown in red and gain in blue, with ringed patches (#N for loss, +N for gain) on the result image, the map and the web page. The program reports the affected area in hectares and the number of patches. It also gives every loss patch a confidence score (based on size, strength of the drop, persistence on later dates and HH agreement) and explains the reasons for it.

Results You Can See

  • A before/after swipe, a time animation, per-patch signal charts and a polarization comparison (HV, HH, HV/HH)
  • Several visualizations of every date: RGB (red, green, blue colour composite), HV and HH in decibels (dB), HV and HH linear, because different channels reveal different things
  • A web map with extra context: ESA WorldCover land cover under the radar, distance of loss patches to roads from OSM (OpenStreetMap), the GFW (Global Forest Watch) tree cover loss layer, and one-click links to Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 for every patch
  • A report in Ukrainian and English with hypotheses about physical and human drivers of the change and future uses of NISAR
  • Saved patches with notes, plus CSV (comma-separated values) and GeoJSON (a map data format) export

Sentinel-1 Cross-Check

SilvaSAR can verify NISAR detections with Sentinel-1, a European radar satellite in the C-band (shorter wavelength). It orders Sentinel-1 RTC (Radiometrically Terrain Corrected) products from ASF HyP3 (Hybrid Pluggable Processing Pipeline) for the dates closest to the NISAR pair. It then tests whether the VH signal also drops inside NISAR loss patches, compared with the rest of the forest. The result appears on the web page as C✓ or C✗ for each patch. Processing runs on the server and needs an Earthdata login.

Built to Be Understood

  • Help at every step. Next to many functions there is a “?” button that explains what the setting does and how to interpret it, so no radar expertise is required.
  • A colour key for the map. Colour markers explain what each colour on the result means (red for loss, blue for gain, and so on).
  • Saved places. All settings (area, thresholds, resolution, minimum patch size, forest threshold, polarization, smoothing, search mode, period) are remembered, and picking a place restores them.
  • Honest about uncertainty. Thresholds are heuristic and not yet validated with field data. Harvest, ploughing, soil moisture and flooding can give a similar signal, and with two dates there is no confirmation by a later date. Large patches should be confirmed with Sentinel-2 or on the ground.

Benefits

  • Detects forest loss early, in any weather and at night
  • Shows not only what changed, but also when, thanks to the time series
  • Saves time: instead of manually analysing gigabytes of radar data, the user gets numbers in hectares and a ranked list of places to check, each with a confidence score
  • Cross-checks results with a second radar band and gives context (land cover, roads, existing tree-loss data), which helps to separate real loss from false alarms
  • Open source (MIT licence) and based on free, open data, so it is accessible to ecologists, foresters, NGOs (non-governmental organizations), local communities, researchers and students
  • Viewing results needs no registration or installation

Our Goal

My goal is to make radar-based forest monitoring simple and accessible to anyone, and to show what NISAR L-band data can do for protecting forests, starting with my region, the Carpathians in Ukraine. I want people to be able to see in a few clicks where trees disappeared and where they are regrowing, and to know how reliable each detection is. In the future I plan to validate the thresholds with field data, reduce false alarms, and extend the forest mask to other polarizations and regions.

Tech Stack

  • Language: Python, HTML, JavaScript
  • Desktop app: a graphical user interface (GUI) with a dark theme, an interactive map and a processing pipeline split into separate modules (search and resumable download, processing, report and confidence scoring, fast recomputation and threshold sensitivity)
  • Web viewer: a static web page (HTML) that reads only layers.json and PNG files, published free on GitHub Pages
  • Data: NISAR L2 GCOV (Level 2 Geocoded Polarimetric Covariance) in the L-band from NASA ASF; Sentinel-1 RTC from ASF HyP3 (C-band); ESA WorldCover; Global Forest Watch; OpenStreetMap
  • Basemaps: Esri, OpenStreetMap, OpenTopoMap and Sentinel-2 cloudless by EOX
  • Outputs: CSV, GeoJSON, reports in Ukrainian and English, and a web map
  • Hardware and tools: a regular Windows PC (no special hardware), Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub
